questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Name TWO types of communication systems that can be used by business organisations to enhance discussions between members of the organisation. (2 marks)

(b) For any of the systems in (a), discuss how it functions, stating clearly the hardware and software required. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Two communication systems (2 marks).** *Video conferencing* and *electronic mail (e-mail)*. (Other accepted answers: instant messaging / chat, audio conferencing or VoIP, an intranet discussion forum.)

**(b) How video conferencing works (2 marks).**

*Functioning.* At each site a camera and a microphone capture the picture and the voice of the participants. The conferencing software compresses (encodes) the audio and video into digital data and sends it in packets over the network or the Internet to the other sites, where it is decompressed (decoded) and shown on a screen or projector and played through loudspeakers, practically in real time. Several members of the organisation in different towns can therefore see, hear and talk to one another, and also share documents or the screen, without travelling.

*Hardware required.* Computers (or smartphones), a webcam (video camera), a microphone, loudspeakers or headset, a screen or projector, a network connection with enough bandwidth (router, modem) and, for large rooms, a codec unit.

*Software required.* A video-conferencing application (for example Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet or Skype) with its audio/video codecs, plus an operating system and the device drivers for the camera and the sound card.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following and in each case illustrate ONE situation where they can be useful.

(a) Computer simulation. (3 marks)

(b) Control system. (3 marks)

(c) Robots. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Computer simulation (3 marks).** *Definition:* the use of a computer program that contains a mathematical model of a real system or process, in order to study how the real system would behave when the data or conditions are changed, without having to build or try the real thing. *Useful situation:* a **flight simulator** used to train pilots, which reproduces take-off, landing and emergencies without any risk or fuel cost. (Others: crash-test simulation for car design, weather forecasting, testing a bridge design, training in medicine.)

**(b) Control system (3 marks).** *Definition:* a system in which a computer (or microprocessor) receives data from **sensors**, processes it against stored values (set points) and sends signals to **actuators** (motors, valves, heaters) in order to regulate a physical process automatically, usually with **feedback** from the output. *Useful situation:* the automatic **temperature control** of a greenhouse or of an air conditioner: a temperature sensor sends readings to the processor; if the temperature is above the set value the processor switches on the fan or cooling, and switches it off when the value is reached. (Others: traffic lights, automatic doors, an ABS braking system.)

**(c) Robots (3 marks).** *Definition:* programmable, computer-controlled machines, fitted with sensors and with mechanical arms or wheels (actuators), that carry out physical tasks automatically and repeatedly. *Useful situation:* on a **car assembly line**, robots weld and paint the bodies quickly, accurately and without tiring; they can also work in places dangerous for people, such as a bomb-disposal robot. (Others: packing in factories, space or deep-sea exploration.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Apart from feasibility studies, outline two other activities involved in the investigation phase of the SDLC. (2 marks)

(b) Describe the different types of feasibility studies carried out in the investigation phase of the SDLC. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Two other activities of the investigation phase (2 marks).**

1. **Fact finding:** collecting information about the present system and the users' needs by interviews, questionnaires, observation of the workers and examination of documents (forms, reports).
2. **Studying the existing system and defining the problem and requirements:** analysing how the present system works, finding its weaknesses and writing down the objectives and the user requirements of the new system. (Another accepted activity: preparing the feasibility report / terms of reference for management.)

**(b) Types of feasibility study (2 marks).** A feasibility study decides whether the proposed system is worth developing. The main types are:

- **Technical feasibility:** do the hardware, software and technical skills needed exist or can they be obtained?
- **Economic feasibility (cost-benefit analysis):** do the benefits of the new system outweigh its development and running costs?
- **Operational feasibility:** will the system work in the organisation and will the users accept and be able to use it?
- **Schedule (time) feasibility:** can the system be finished within the time allowed?
- **Legal feasibility:** does the system respect the law (data protection, licences, contracts)?
